title: Mardana and the rebab
hook: a Muslim musician, Bhai Mardana, becomes his lifelong companion; Mardana plays and Nanak sings

segments.voice: Yesterday: the qazi, and a mind that had wandered home to a young horse. Your line: where is your mind right now.

Guru Nanak had a partner, the player whose hands made the song work. His name was Mardana. He came from Nanak's own village, Talwandi, and tradition says he was about ten years older. He was a Muslim, from a family of hereditary musicians, the kind who played at weddings and sang the genealogies of the village. And he carried an instrument everywhere he went. When Nanak came out of the river with something to say, Mardana gave it a tune.
screen: `NANAK HAD A PARTNER.` → `A MUSLIM MUSICIAN FROM TALWANDI.` → `HE CARRIED AN INSTRUMENT.`

segments.voice: The instrument was a rebab: plucked strings, a wooden body, skin stretched across the front, and a deep, woody voice. It's the ancestor, or at least a cousin, of instruments played across Central and South Asia today. Here's how the two of them worked. Nanak would feel a hymn coming, and tradition says he'd turn to his friend with something like: Mardana, play the rebab, the Word is coming. Mardana found the note, and Nanak sang. So Sikh scripture didn't begin as something read silently. It was born as music. That's why the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raga, by musical mode, and why, in a gurdwara today, the hymns are still sung to instruments. Now look at who's holding the rebab. A Muslim musician sat at the side of a teacher born into a Hindu family, and for years they walked together, ate together and slept on the same roads. There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim: Mardana is that line with a face and a pair of hands. Sikhs still honor him by name. A few verses in the scripture carry his name, and, tradition says, his descendants, the rababis, sang the hymns in Sikh gatherings for generations. Neither of them did it alone. The words needed the music, and the music needed the words. With this, the early years close: the boy at Talwandi, the river, the storehouse, the first words after.
screen: `THE REBAB — STRINGS, SKIN, WOOD.` · `MARDANA, PLAY. THE WORD IS COMING.` · `SCRIPTURE BORN AS MUSIC.` · `A MUSLIM MUSICIAN AT NANAK'S SIDE.` · then, large: `ONE PLAYS, ONE SINGS.`

segments.voice: Put on one piece of music, any music, or let the bell's two minutes be the music, and listen all the way through, doing nothing else; stay even through the part you usually skip. Listen for the instrument underneath the voice, the one you normally don't hear. Somebody is playing it, so the singer can sing.
Rebab. The stringed instrument Bhai Mardana played beside Guru Nanak, so the hymns could be sung. Today's word.
Your line: one plays, one sings. Tomorrow the two of them walk out of town. Day thirty-one.

howItsDone: Sikh hymns are sung, not only read: in gurdwaras, musicians called ragis sing the scripture to instruments in the ragas it is arranged by, and Bhai Mardana is remembered as the Guru's own musician.

chat.says: Why is Sikh scripture sung with instruments instead of just read?
options: It was born as music: Mardana played the rebab while Nanak sang.
Instruments came centuries later, to make long readings less tiring.
Mardana wrote the tunes down first, and Nanak fit words to them later.
chat.meaning: Nanak would say the Word was coming, Mardana found the note, and Nanak sang. That's why the scripture is arranged by raga.

notes: Mardana's age (about ten years older than Nanak) and his family as Mirasi hereditary musicians follow common tradition; confirm.
The saying 'Mardana, play the rebab, the Word is coming' is a janamsakhi motif, paraphrased; confirm the framing.

Saloks headed 'Mardana 1' in Bihagare ki Var (around Ang 553): whether they are addressed to Mardana or composed in his name is read differently; voice now says only that a few verses carry his name. Confirm Ang and framing.
Rababis (Mardana's descendants) as kirtan singers until the twentieth century; confirm.
Rebab described as the ancestor or cousin of instruments across Central and South Asia; kept deliberately loose. Confirm.
